findings.body:
Removing `@require_role("admin")` leaves `DELETE /users/<user>` with no access control. Any client that can reach this route can delete any user (`USERS.remove(user)` → 204), including admins.

Cleanup jobs hitting 403 should get a dedicated principal or role (e.g. `service` / `cleanup`) checked on the **caller**, or the job should authenticate as admin — not an open endpoint.

Restore a role check (or equivalent authn/authz) before merge; do not ship an unauthenticated destructive route.

summary:
## Verdict

**Critical authorization bypass** — `DELETE /users/<user>` is now callable with no role check, so any client can delete any user.

## Narrative

The PR removes `@require_role("admin")` from `delete_user` to unblock cleanup jobs that run as a viewer. That trades a 403 for an open delete endpoint: there is no replacement gate (caller auth, service-account role, or internal-only binding).

`require_role` still exists in `app.py` and is the only access control on this route. After this change, `delete_user` only does `USERS.remove(user)` and returns 204. Anyone who can reach the app can remove `alice`, `bob`, or any other name in the list.

A durable fix is to authorize the **caller** (or a dedicated cleanup/service role), not to drop the decorator. If cleanup must run as `viewer`, add an explicit role or principal that is allowed to delete, and keep denying anonymous or unrelated callers.

## Release decision

**Recommendation:** request-changes

verification.reason: Base had `@require_role("admin")` on `DELETE /users/<user>`; head replaces it with a comment and leaves `delete_user` with no auth check before `USERS.remove(user)` → 204. Any reachable client can delete any user, so the critical authorization regression holds.
